title: Toms Divorce

jokes.text: They put a popcorn machine up there just to brighten things up, but they used the wrong kind of oil and a bunch of people had to get their throats replaced.
jokes.setup: The fourth floor is established as a miserable place; someone tried to improve morale with a popcorn machine
jokes.punchline: The oil was wrong, and people had to get their THROATS REPLACED — an absurdly medical escalation of a mundane hazard
jokes.explanation: The joke earns its high score through a perfectly executed misdirection: the setup of a cheerful popcorn machine is utterly benign, then catastrophically derailed by 'their throats replaced' — a clinically specific, medically absurd consequence that sounds almost plausible in a governmental hellscape. It's extremely quotable and pure Leslie Knope: well-intentioned government initiatives spiraling into disaster. One of the episode's best constructed jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The fourth floor? That's the creepiest place on earth.

jokes.text: Because I don't want to. (Leslie's real reason she can't go to the fourth floor)
jokes.setup: Leslie insists someone else must go because 'I can't go'
jokes.punchline: Her reason is simply 'Because I don't want to' — undercutting her authority entirely
jokes.explanation: The comedic reveal that Leslie's official-sounding 'can't' is just 'won't' is a great character beat. Perfectly economical and very true to her personality. The misdirection is simple but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The fourth floor is creepy because there's a popcorn machine that hasn't been emptied since 1987.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's not creepy, that's just gross.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Plus there's a guy up there who does unlicensed throat replacement surgery.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Now that's creepy.

jokes.text: Hey, boo, you're pretty. / Are you on probation? / I got clean urine. You need female, I got female.
jokes.setup: Ann arrives on the fourth floor, which has been built up as a terrifying den of societal misery
jokes.punchline: She is immediately hit on and offered clean urine by a stranger who also offers to buy hers — confirming every horrible expectation
jokes.explanation: A solid payoff to the setup about the fourth floor. The specificity of the clean urine offer — and the escalation to 'I buy too' — takes a predictable 'weird place' joke and gives it a weird transactional twist that elevates it. The comedic payoff is satisfying because it exceeds but validates the setup.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't go to the zoning meeting. Tom, you have to go instead.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Why can't you go?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because I don't want to.

jokes.text: Took a risk, bought some shoes online. Paid off handsomely, as you can see.
jokes.setup: Leslie gently probes Tom about how things are going in his life
jokes.punchline: Tom's highlight of his week is internet shoe shopping, delivered with maximum self-satisfaction
jokes.explanation: Pure Tom Haverford character comedy. His unironic pride in a mundane consumer decision, framed as a 'risk,' is perfectly in character and economically delivered. 'Paid off handsomely, as you can see' implies he expects visual admiration for his feet, which is a funny assumed visual beat.

dialogue.speaker: Fourth floor stranger
dialogue.line: Hey man, you look like you could use some clean urine samples.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? No, I'm just trying to find the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Fourth floor stranger
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's what they all say.

jokes.text: Lasted longer than Avril Lavigne and the guy from Sum 41. Am I right?
jokes.setup: Leslie expresses sympathy about Tom's divorce
jokes.punchline: Tom deflects with a pop-culture celebrity comparison that's oddly specific and delivered with breezy confidence
jokes.explanation: The joke works because of Tom's character: his obsession with celebrity culture as a benchmark for real life is spot-on. The tag 'Am I right?' signals he expects validation for an oddly specific comparison. Leslie's 'I don't know what those are' is a perfect straight-man response.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Everything's great! You know, I've been really focusing on the important things in life. Like my shoe game. I just copped these limited edition sneakers from a boutique in SoHo. They're Italian leather, handcrafted, cost more than my first car. Life is all about the details, you know?

jokes.text: I don't know what those are. (Leslie's response to Tom's Avril Lavigne/Sum 41 reference)
jokes.setup: Tom references Avril Lavigne and the guy from Sum 41 as a cultural touchstone
jokes.punchline: Leslie has no idea who either of those people are, puncturing Tom's attempt at relatability
jokes.explanation: A clean character-based punchline. Leslie's total ignorance of early 2000s pop-punk is perfectly in character and deflates Tom's confident pop-culture posturing in one economical line. Good straight-man work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, it's not a big deal. Divorce happens. It's like when... you know, it's basically the same as when Brad Pitt and that one actress were together for like three weeks. Nobody really noticed, nobody really cared.

jokes.text: I did a little research, and divorce is the number two most stressful event in a person's life. Of course marriage is number seven. So watch out, everyone. It's all bad.
jokes.setup: Leslie has researched divorce to better support Tom
jokes.punchline: Her research leads her to a bleak, universally pessimistic conclusion about marriage itself — 'It's all bad' — delivered matter-of-factly
jokes.explanation: This is excellent Leslie Knope joke construction. Her earnest, research-based approach to a personal crisis, combined with the perfectly logical but hilariously nihilistic conclusion — 'So watch out, everyone. It's all bad.' — is quintessential Parks and Rec. The pivot from caring to bleak is sharp and the delivery arc is perfectly structured. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, Sum 41? Is that a math problem? Like, the sum of 41 what?

jokes.text: Tom always seems like Mr. Slickster cool guy, but he's hiding his emotions underneath a very thick layer of axe body spray.
jokes.setup: Leslie argues Tom is not as fine as he seems
jokes.punchline: The metaphor of hiding emotions under Axe body spray — a very Tom-specific detail — is the unexpected specificity that makes it land
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific comedy. The joke lands because 'Axe body spray' is both a literal and metaphorical truth about Tom — it's exactly the kind of surface-level image management he performs. Leslie's earnest delivery of the metaphor makes it even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It would have been nice to save your marriage.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I tried to fix it myself first. Unplugged it, plugged it back in. Didn't work. Then I called tech support, but they said the warranty had expired.

jokes.text: Don't be all like, 'I don't want to. I am a guy, and I like fire and playing hockey and eating meat. No, no, says I.' — Leslie's impression of Ron
jokes.setup: Leslie is telling Ron not to be dismissive of emotional support for Tom
jokes.punchline: She does a hilariously reductive impression of generic masculine resistance, with the oddly formal 'No, no, says I' as the topper
jokes.explanation: The impression works on multiple levels: it's funny as a parody of masculine emotional avoidance, it's funny because the archaic 'No, no, says I' is so incongruously formal, and it's great Leslie Knope character work — she'd absolutely rehearse this kind of rhetorical impression. Ron's understated acknowledgment ('That was a really good Ron') is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I was doing research on divorce stress, and it turns out marriage is also incredibly stressful. So it's all bad.

jokes.text: None of his family lives here, and all of his friends are frat guys and morons.
jokes.setup: Ron is reluctantly agreeing with Leslie's point about helping Tom.
jokes.punchline: Ron's blunt assessment of Tom's social circle — 'frat guys and morons' — delivered with complete Ron Swanson flatness, is both insulting and probably accurate.
jokes.explanation: Ron's delivery — factual, unsentimental, economical — makes this work. He's technically being supportive but frames Tom's entire social life as pathetic. Classic Ron Swanson: help delivered as mild contempt.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom seems fine, but he's not fine. He's like a bottle of Axe body spray – all aggressive confidence on the outside, but deep down, he's just masking a very sad, very lonely smell.

jokes.text: That was a really good Ron. / Thank you.
jokes.setup: Leslie does her Ron impression and awaits pushback
jokes.punchline: Ron sincerely compliments the impression of himself, then Leslie accepts the compliment without irony
jokes.explanation: This two-line exchange is nearly perfect sitcom economy. Ron praising the accuracy of an impression mocking him — without defensiveness or irony — is pure Ron Swanson. And Leslie's gracious 'Thank you' doubles down on the absurdity. The whole joke lives in the characters; it couldn't work with anyone else. Very high character integration score is warranted.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Don't be unsupportive. I'm doing this thing and I need you all behind me. And I mean that literally and figuratively.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I don't need any of that negativity. That's just... *puts hands on hips, deepens voice* 'Oh, Leslie, that'll never work. You're crazy. You're a woman and you can't do that.' That's what I'm talking about.

jokes.text: Hey, Mark. The shoeshine stand still doesn't have that syphilis medication you were asking about.
jokes.setup: Ann arrives at the office — ostensibly for innocent, relationship-related reasons
jokes.punchline: Andy publicly announces that the shoeshine stand doesn't have Mark's syphilis medication, a completely fabricated and humiliating claim
jokes.explanation: The joke is a great Andy Dwyer moment — his relationship sabotage campaign is childish and petty, and announcing fake STI medication at a workplace is perfectly embarrassing. The specificity of 'syphilis' (not just 'medication') and the mundane setting of a shoeshine stand adds wonderful absurdist texture.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Waffles. Breakfast food. Government. No nonsense.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's Ron.

jokes.text: What a coincidence. Are you in this office purely for business reasons? / Pleasure, actually. My boyfriend, Mark, works here.
jokes.setup: Ann appears at the office again — seemingly coincidentally
jokes.punchline: Mark's sarcastically polite inquiry and Ann's breezy, innocent answer expose that she's definitely there for non-business reasons
jokes.explanation: Competent but not exceptional. The joke relies on Mark's resigned exasperation and Ann's obliviousness, which is a functional dynamic but not particularly original or sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey everyone, I need to let you all know that I have a very serious medical condition. I'm gonna need to take frequent bathroom breaks because of my... uh... explosive diarrhea.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Also, I'm gonna need some privacy because I have a really bad case of hemorrhoids. And I'm gonna be wearing a diaper for the next few weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, and one more thing - I have a fungal infection that's really, really contagious, so nobody should come near me. Thanks for understanding, everybody!

jokes.text: What a surprise running into you all day every day every single place that we are.
jokes.setup: Andy shows up (again) at the office while Mark and Ann are there
jokes.punchline: Mark's escalating, exhausted sarcasm about Andy's constant presence builds to the absurd 'every single place that we are'
jokes.explanation: Mark's deadpan escalation works well — the threefold structure ('all day / every day / every single place that we are') has good internal rhythm. A solid mid-tier joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy, you can't keep showing up at my workplace.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Why not? I like seeing you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Because it's unprofessional. You showed up at my last job, and the one before that.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So? Andy, you do this everywhere. Every single place that we are.

jokes.text: Also, Mark, again, we don't have those extra-small condoms you ordered. I called the factory. It's gonna take a special order. Not just because of the size, but because of the weird shape as well. Something they've never dealt with before.
jokes.setup: Andy already planted a fake syphilis medication rumor; now he returns with a follow-up fake insult
jokes.punchline: Extra-small, weirdly-shaped condoms that require a factory special order — with each clause making it more specific and more devastating
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is excellent — each new detail ('extra-small,' 'weird shape,' 'something they've never dealt with before') piles on perfectly. The callback nature makes it funnier than the original, and 'We'll talk' as a button is a great understatement topper. Andy's cheerful obliviousness while delivering devastating insults is pure character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm escalating this. I'm going to order a pizza, but I'm going to request a weird shape.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Like, not a circle, not a square. Something that's going to require them to consult with the factory.

jokes.text: Every day I subtly chip away at their relationship, weakening it little by little. (Andy's confessional)
jokes.setup: Andy has been planting embarrassing fake rumors about Mark
jokes.punchline: His confessional reveal that this is a deliberate long-term strategy — 'subtly' — delivered with complete sincerity, is the joke. The strategy is obviously not subtle at all.
jokes.explanation: The word 'subtly' is doing enormous comic work here. Andy's syphilis and weird-condom announcements are the opposite of subtle, yet he describes his campaign with the language of a patient strategist. This ironic self-assessment, delivered in earnest confessional mode, is excellent character comedy. High character integration: this only works because it's Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've been very subtle about this whole thing. Very subtle. I mean, nobody suspects me at all.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've left no evidence. I've covered my tracks perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I basically whispered when I yelled about it, and I wore a fake mustache that I drew on with a Sharpie.

jokes.text: So, Tom... / So you had a divorce / Of course of course / And no one enjoys a divorce of course — Leslie's Mr. Ed parody song
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to locate Tom to support him
jokes.punchline: She breaks into a spontaneous parody song to the tune of 'Mr. Ed' about Tom's divorce — a completely unhinged response to a routine situation
jokes.explanation: A delightful Leslie Knope absurdist moment. Her impulse to communicate through a TV theme song parody is pure character, and the content ('no one enjoys a divorce of course') is bleak enough to be funny. The joke relies heavily on performance and the absurdity of the choice itself.

jokes.text: Leslie thinks you're a wounded animal, so her female instincts are kicking in. Here's what you do. Act sad. Let her pull the thorn out of your paw and wrap a bandage around it. That'll make her feel better. She'll get off your jock.
jokes.setup: Tom is frustrated that Leslie won't leave him alone about his divorce
jokes.punchline: Ron delivers a piece of pragmatic, unsentimental advice using an oddly tender animal metaphor, then punctures it with 'She'll get off your jock'
jokes.explanation: Ron Swanson at his best: the advice is genuinely practical and compassionate at its core, but delivered in the most transactional, unemotional terms possible. The thorn-in-paw metaphor has unexpected gentleness, then 'She'll get off your jock' obliterates any warmth. Only Ron Swanson says this. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, I just wanted to thank you for that advice. It really helped me out.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, you're like the Condoleezza Rice of business advice. Ron-doleezza Rice.

jokes.text: Thanks, Rondoleezza Rice.
jokes.setup: Tom thanks Ron for his advice
jokes.punchline: He calls Ron 'Rondoleezza Rice' — blending Ron's name with Condoleezza Rice's — a spontaneous, absurd nickname
jokes.explanation: A gem of economy. Tom's habit of giving people absurd nicknames is in character, and 'Rondoleezza Rice' is a genuinely clever wordplay that fuses Ron's name with a female political figure — implying Ron's advice was so good it transcended his gruff masculinity. Very quotable, very Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: We could watch a documentary about tandem bicycles.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That sounds unapologetic.

jokes.text: There's a really fun documentary about tandem bicycles at the art house. Supposed to be pretty unapologetic.
jokes.setup: Everyone is brainstorming where to take Tom for a fun night out
jokes.punchline: Leslie's idea of a fun night for a recently divorced man is a 'pretty unapologetic' documentary about tandem bicycles
jokes.explanation: The joke lives in the word 'unapologetic' applied to a documentary about tandem bicycles — a subject that has nothing to be apologetic about. This is perfect Leslie character comedy: her earnest enthusiasm for something completely inappropriate to the situation. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: A strip club?

dialogue.speaker: Others
dialogue.line: No, no, Jerry, we're not going to a strip club.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: But you said strip club.

dialogue.speaker: Others
dialogue.line: We didn't say that.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm pretty sure you said strip club.

jokes.text: Strip club? / Did somebody say strip club? / No. / Somebody say strip club? / You did. / I definitely heard someone say strip club. / You did.
jokes.setup: The group is debating where to go, with Leslie suggesting a documentary
jokes.punchline: Tom/Jerry immediately jump to strip club; when told no one suggested it, they insist someone did — a running denial loop
jokes.explanation: A functional, crowd-pleasing bit. The repeated insistence that 'someone' suggested strip club when it was clearly the speaker is a reliable comedy structure. Not particularly original but well-executed rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I recommend Jurassic Fork. It's a steakhouse with dinosaur decorations.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I eat there four times a week.

jokes.text: Would the glitter factory be okay with whoever suggested strip club?
jokes.setup: The strip club suggestion has been made; Leslie is a self-described feminist
jokes.punchline: She refers to the strip club as 'the glitter factory' — a euphemism that reveals she knows exactly what it is and has a nickname for it
jokes.explanation: 'The Glitter Factory' is a great name for a strip club and an even better joke about Leslie's character. The fact that she has a specific name for a local strip club — while framing her question in formal procedural language ('would the glitter factory be okay with whoever suggested') — is brilliant. It implies history she'd never admit to. Highly quotable and rewatch-worthy for the implications alone.

dialogue.speaker: Server
dialogue.line: How would you like your steak cooked?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Medium roar.

dialogue.speaker: Server
dialogue.line: Medium rare?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No. Medium roar. This is a dinosaur restaurant, isn't it?

jokes.text: There is a great dinosaur-themed restaurant in Patterson. It is called Jurassic Fork. I have gone there three times a week for the last 15 years.
jokes.setup: The group needs a dinner destination that isn't a strip club
jokes.punchline: Ron — the stoic, masculine meat enthusiast — has been religiously attending a dinosaur-themed novelty restaurant three times a week for 15 years
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The reveal has perfect structure: Ron Swanson — the ultimate embodiment of grim masculine practicality — has been devoutly attending a children's dinosaur restaurant for 15 years. The name 'Jurassic Fork' is a great pun. His deadpan delivery ('three times a week for the last 15 years') without any self-consciousness is pure Ron. The joke couldn't belong to any other character. This approaches the top of the episode's range.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I'll have the saurus-aged steak.

dialogue.speaker: Server
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, sir, we can't use dinosaur puns. We have a cease and desist from the Jurassic Park people.

jokes.text: Hi, welcome to Jurassic Fork where the only thing that'll be extinct is your appetite.
jokes.setup: The group arrives at the dinosaur-themed restaurant Ron loves
jokes.punchline: The scripted greeting is an earnest, terrible dinosaur pun — the restaurant takes itself completely seriously
jokes.explanation: A solid theme restaurant joke. 'The only thing that'll be extinct is your appetite' is a competent, corny pun that works because the restaurant is played completely straight. The earnestness is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: When we split bills, I always say, 'Hey, don't be a cheap-o-saurus Rex!' But then I actually am a cheap-o-saurus Rex.

jokes.text: I will have the Jamaican jerk chicken veloci-wrap. / I'm gonna get the tricera-chops, please.
jokes.setup: The group orders food at the dinosaur-themed restaurant
jokes.punchline: The menu items are all dinosaur puns — 'veloci-wrap,' 'tricera-chops' — delivered deadpan as if normal
jokes.explanation: The running gag of dinosaur menu puns is consistently funny because each new pun is a small discovery. 'Veloci-wrap' and 'tricera-chops' are solid entries in the bit.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what they say - sometimes the best way to get someone to do what you want is to appeal to their sense of self-worth and make them feel like they're making their own decision.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, did that actually work?

jokes.text: How do you want that cooked? / Medium roar. / Medium rare? / No, medium roar. / For legal reasons, we can't make puns about the temperature of the meats.
jokes.setup: Ann is ordering at Jurassic Fork
jokes.punchline: Ann tries to order 'medium roar' as a temperature pun; the server clarifies they legally cannot do that — implying actual legal proceedings over dinosaur meat temperature puns
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. The premise that there's a LEGAL reason the restaurant can't pun on meat temperatures — implying someone was sued or regulated over 'medium roar' — is inspired absurdism. The server's deadpan seriousness about this completely insane policy makes it land perfectly. High originality: this specific comedic premise is genuinely novel. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Wow, Tom, you've been working out. You're looking really fit.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Why? What do you know? Did someone say something? Am I a suspect?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: No, I'm just giving you a compliment.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, that's how it starts. Next thing you know, they're asking about my whereabouts on specific dates.

jokes.text: I'll have the surf and turf-osaurus, and a couple of bottles of wine? I'm gonna need a lot of wine, so keep it flowing.
jokes.setup: Tom is performing sadness about his divorce as part of Ron's strategy
jokes.punchline: He orders dramatically, tacking 'and a couple of bottles of wine' onto a dinosaur pun order — a diva move at a children's restaurant
jokes.explanation: The joke is Tom performing melodramatic sadness at a ridiculous venue. It's a good character beat but the 'surf and turf-osaurus' pun is doing most of the work.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I've been working out. What do you think?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's... weird.

jokes.text: I'm not a big fan of group dinners where everybody splits the bill no matter what they get. I ordered a tyranno-ceasar salad, and that's all I'm paying for.
jokes.setup: The group is having a 'Tom's night' dinner
jokes.punchline: April breaks from the emotional occasion to make a petty statement about bill-splitting, punctuated by the pun 'tyranno-ceasar salad'
jokes.explanation: Great April Ludgate character moment — her refusal to engage with the emotional context in favor of petty pragmatics is on point. The 'tyranno-ceasar salad' pun is also a good addition to the restaurant's running gag.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Tom, you're the least terrible person here. Everyone else is basically garbage.

jokes.text: How to hustle somebody in pool by Andy Dwyer. Step 1, find the person you want to hustle. Invite them to play pool. Should they accept, you're in.
jokes.setup: Andy challenges Mark to pool, announcing his intention to hustle him
jokes.punchline: His 'Step 1' is comically basic — the strategy is essentially 'challenge someone to pool' — delivering it with the gravitas of a genuine con man's tutorial
jokes.explanation: This confessional beat is sharp. The joke is entirely structural: Andy frames his 'hustle' in the language of sophisticated strategy, but Step 1 is just 'ask someone to play pool. If they say yes, you're in.' The anti-climax is perfectly executed, and the earnest delivery is pure Andy. Excellent character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Tom, you're like a little puppy dog.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, thank you, Donna!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: A puppy dog that's learning to use the toilet for the first time.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay...

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: And you're so proud of yourself, you run around showing everyone the toilet, and they're like, 'Yes, Tom, you did it!'

jokes.text: Finally settle that debate about who's the better pool player. / I've never had that debate with anyone.
jokes.setup: Andy approaches Mark at the pool table and invites him to play.
jokes.punchline: Andy frames the game as resolving a long-standing debate; Mark flatly notes that debate has never existed.
jokes.explanation: Clean two-line joke. Andy's invention of a fake rivalry to justify a hustle, and Mark's flat denial, is well-timed and economical. Sets up the pool subplot efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm gonna need another round of wings, some loaded nachos, and honestly, just bring the whole dessert menu. I'm going through a really rough time right now.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You could say my life is... extinct. Like the dinosaurs. Which is sad. But also kind of cool when you think about it.

jokes.text: Here's what I think we should do. Everyone should go around and say one thing that they love about Tom. / I really wish I could have your body. / What? / Like, tied up, naked, in your basement?
jokes.setup: Leslie proposes a nice group activity to make Tom feel loved
jokes.punchline: Jerry's compliment starts sweetly ambiguous ('I really wish I could have your body') then Tom's horrified interpretation ('tied up, naked, in your basement?') makes it suddenly dark
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection: the line 'I wish I could have your body' is an innocent fitness compliment, but the immediate interpretation — which is the audience's reading too — goes somewhere much darker. Tom voicing the dark interpretation out loud is excellent. Jerry's harmless follow-up ('I mean, you're in good shape') completes the joke well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I genuinely cannot fathom why Tom would pretend to be sad. Like, who does that? Who wakes up and thinks, 'You know what would really help my day? Pretending to be depressed so people pay attention to me.' It's insane. It's such an insane thing to do.

jokes.text: No, I mean, you're in good shape, and you can eat whatever you want. Well, that was weird, Jerry.
jokes.setup: Jerry clarifies his body compliment; the situation was briefly sinister
jokes.punchline: Leslie summarizes the moment as 'weird, Jerry' — confirming the room's discomfort while Jerry is completely oblivious to what he did
jokes.explanation: A serviceable button on the Jerry joke. 'That was weird, Jerry' is a very Parks and Rec line. Not exceptional on its own but works as a topper.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna go in there and absolutely destroy these guys at pool. I've got this whole strategy worked out. I'm gonna lean back, look real cool, maybe do some trick shots...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, Mark's really good at pool.

jokes.text: I love you, Tom. You're my little prince. Just want to put you in a little cape and a little hat and just fly you around.
jokes.setup: Group members are saying what they love about Tom
jokes.punchline: Donna's affection is expressed by wanting to put Tom in a tiny cape and hat and fly him around — weirdly physical, maternally absurd imagery
jokes.explanation: Donna's love for Tom expressed as wanting to shrink him and accessorize him is a delightfully specific form of affection. The repetition of 'little' is well-calibrated for maximum absurdity. Strong Donna character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Women are always crying. It's like their thing.

jokes.text: I'm still feeling pretty sad. Can I get two creme brulees and another glass of 'bronto' grigio?
jokes.setup: Tom is performing sadness to get pity from the group
jokes.punchline: 'Bronto' grigio — Tom adapts 'pinot grigio' into a dinosaur pun while ordering, perfectly in the spirit of the restaurant AND revealing he's having a fine time
jokes.explanation: A great moment because it does multiple things: it's a good dinosaur pun ('bronto' grigio), it reveals Tom is thoroughly enjoying himself while performing misery, and the two crème brulées is a nice bit of excess. The joke rewards attention.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Wendy has a lot of positive qualities. She's intelligent, she's driven, she's got strong bone structure. Her shoulders are very broad—good for childbearing. And her teeth are... adequate.

jokes.text: I thought I had Tom all figured out, but it's almost like he's faking being sad. Why would he do that? (Leslie's confessional)
jokes.setup: Tom is very obviously performing sadness to get sympathy and free food
jokes.punchline: Leslie, the ostensibly perceptive protagonist, is completely baffled by what the audience can plainly see
jokes.explanation: A competent dramatic irony moment. Leslie's obliviousness is a recurring comedy engine, and it works here. Not exceptional, but solid.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what? I think I didn't really think this through.

jokes.text: Step two, lose to your opponent intentionally, so they gain confidence. Step two has been completed. Easily. Very easily. Mark is pretty good at pool.
jokes.setup: Andy is narrating his pool hustle strategy
jokes.punchline: Step two was to lose intentionally — but his confessionals reveal he actually just lost, badly, and is scrambling to reframe it
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural payoff. The joke works because Andy's confessional re-frames his actual humiliating loss as the intended Step Two. 'Mark is pretty good at pool' — delivered flat, after claiming he was letting Mark win — is perfect. The escalating qualifiers ('Easily. Very easily.') trying to sell the lie make it even better. Great callback and character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna put up my limited edition Duran Duran t-shirt from 1986.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not worth anything.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Not worth anything? I got this shirt at a Duran Duran concert. I was there with my dad. He got drunk and fell into the mosh pit. Security had to fish him out. He threw up on my shoes. I had to walk around the rest of the concert barefoot. I stepped on a broken bottle and had to get seven stitches. Then Duran Duran came out for the encore, and Simon Le Bon looked right at me, and I swear he winked. So this shirt represents one of the most important nights of my life.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Still not worth anything.

jokes.text: Now that you're getting divorced, I sort of feel like there may be some potential with me and Wendy. Would it be okay with you if I was to ask her out once the fake dust settles? ... She might be the perfect spooning size for me.
jokes.setup: Ron has been helping Tom get through his divorce
jokes.punchline: Ron asks Tom's permission to pursue Wendy, framing his romantic interest in the clinical language of logistics. The kicker: his criterion for compatibility is 'the perfect spooning size.'
jokes.explanation: Ron Swanson expressing romantic interest through the language of physical logistics ('perfect spooning size') is one of the episode's best character moments. It subverts expectations: we might expect Ron to be awkward about asking, but he's completely matter-of-fact. 'Spooning size' as a romantic criterion is both funny and oddly sweet. Extremely high character integration — this is only funny because it's Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, okay. Let's make this fair. What if we both put something on the line?

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Alright, I'm in. What do you want to bet?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'll put up my dirt bike.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I'll put up my girlfriend.

jokes.text: That would be $6,400. I accept checks and most major credit cards.
jokes.setup: Andy has been losing money to Mark at pool; the debt has been accumulating
jokes.punchline: The amount is $6,400 — a wildly inflated sum for a pool bet that started small, delivered matter-of-factly by Mark
jokes.explanation: The escalation from a small bet to $6,400 is a good comedic payoff. Mark calmly accepting 'checks and most major credit cards' for a pool game elevates it from a simple number joke to a character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, I will give you a raise.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I will also give you a company car.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wow!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And a goose heart.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A fresh goose heart. Every morning.

jokes.text: Mark is way better than me. I'm gonna say that there is at least a chance that I didn't think this through completely.
jokes.setup: Andy is $6,400 in debt from pool
jokes.punchline: His confessional admission that he 'at least' has a chance he didn't think it through — delivered with masterful understatement — is the punchline
jokes.explanation: 'There is at least a chance that I didn't think this through completely' is beautifully calibrated understatement. The hedging language ('at least a chance') when he's clearly in disaster is excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm a club promoter.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You mean an aspiring club promoter?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I was, until you made me say it.

jokes.text: A t-shirt I tackled Eddie Vedder in. It's literally priceless.
jokes.setup: Andy has no money to bet but wants to keep playing
jokes.punchline: His most valued possession is a t-shirt connected to a violent encounter with a Pearl Jam frontman, which he describes as 'literally priceless'
jokes.explanation: Perfect Andy Dwyer character artifact. That he tackled Eddie Vedder (rather than, say, met him) and considers the shirt 'literally priceless' is wonderfully specific and character-revealing. The joke is Andy's entire value system in one sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom's sadness is just pouring out of him. It's like a brachiosaurus that's been shot with a tranquilizer dart and is slowly collapsing to the ground. And we're all just standing there watching it happen, hoping someone calls a veterinarian.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Which is why we should all go to Jurassic Fork.

jokes.text: So if I win, I also get Ann. / Okay, fine. If you win, then you get Ann.
jokes.setup: Andy can't pay his debt; Mark offers an alternative bet — that Andy stops bothering them
jokes.punchline: Andy escalates by wagering Ann as a prize if he wins, and Mark — in a moment of tired exasperation — agrees to this
jokes.explanation: The joke works on the absurdity of two men casually wagering a woman they both claim to care about in a pool game. It's dark-subversive in that it parodies toxic male behavior while Ann is completely absent. Mark's defeated agreement is the cherry on top — he's too tired to object to the insanity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I can't go to the strip club. Donna found out I used her good microwave to heat up some wings, and now she won't talk to me.

jokes.text: Somebody punch someone. (Leslie's reaction to the pool bet situation)
jokes.setup: The group is watching the absurd pool bet scenario unfold
jokes.punchline: Leslie, watching all this, can only express frustration through a desire for random physical violence
jokes.explanation: A good reaction beat. 'Somebody punch someone' is unexpectedly violent from Leslie and funny for it. Economy is high — three words doing a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm a feminist. I believe in equal pay, reproductive rights, and the right to choose. So if I were a stripper, my name would be Equality.

jokes.text: A cheese fountain? A ruby? A goose heart?
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to cheer up Tom at the restaurant by offering him anything he wants.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's brainstormed suggestions escalate from semi-plausible (cheese fountain) through expensive (a ruby) to genuinely bizarre (a goose heart) — the escalation is funnier than any individual item.
jokes.explanation: The list joke's escalation is well-calibrated: cheese fountain is Leslie-specific (indulgent food), ruby escalates to expensive/romantic, goose heart pivots to something obscure and slightly macabre. Three items, perfectly ordered. 'A goose heart' earns a disproportionate laugh for its brevity.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: This is actually a fascinating study in objectification and the male gaze. I'm here in a purely observational capacity, documenting the sociological implications of—oh my God, is that a dollar bill in her—I mean, the commodification of the human form is really quite remarkable when you think about it from a feminist perspective.

jokes.text: Want some steak? Champagne? Think of something and we'll get it. What do you want? A cheese fountain? A ruby? A goose heart?
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to cheer up Tom at the strip club
jokes.punchline: Her escalating list of gifts ('cheese fountain / a ruby / a goose heart') goes from luxury to absurd to bizarrely specific in rapid succession
jokes.explanation: The list joke escalates perfectly: 'steak' and 'champagne' are normal luxury comfort items, then 'cheese fountain' is absurd, then 'a ruby' is grandiose, then 'a goose heart' comes completely out of nowhere as the final, inexplicable offer. The specificity of 'goose heart' makes it excellent. Very Leslie: her caring manifests in increasingly surreal generosity. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: You know, it's interesting. At a nice restaurant, the waiter brings you water without asking. Here, the dancer won't even make eye contact.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I guess that's the difference between full service and, uh... selective service.

jokes.text: She's a tall, beautiful surgeon. I'm a short, beautiful government employee slash club promoter. / You're a club promoter? / Aspiring.
jokes.setup: Tom is performing sadness and articulating why his marriage to Wendy didn't make sense.
jokes.punchline: Tom describes himself as 'short, beautiful' (a self-compliment buried in self-pity), then 'slash club promoter' draws Leslie's attention, and Tom's correction to 'aspiring' deflates his own resume mid-sentence.
jokes.explanation: Three-part joke: (1) Tom calling himself 'beautiful' while listing a disadvantage, (2) Leslie's natural curiosity about 'club promoter,' (3) Tom's 'Aspiring' deflation. Each beat reveals something true about Tom — his vanity, his ambition, his perpetual gap between self-image and reality. Excellent character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm hiding dollar bills in places so exotic, the Secret Service is gonna think I'm running a money laundering operation.

jokes.text: Now the sadness is pouring out of Tom. Like blood from a pterodactyl after it's attacked by a T-Rex.
jokes.setup: Tom begins expressing genuine emotion about his marriage ending
jokes.punchline: Leslie narrates his sadness using a completely unnecessary dinosaur metaphor, clearly influenced by the evening's theme
jokes.explanation: A great callback to the Jurassic Fork dinner — Leslie has internalized the dinosaur theme and now uses it as her emotional metaphor. That it's completely unnecessary and oddly specific ('pterodactyl... attacked by a T-Rex') is excellent. The joke reveals Leslie's earnest connection between her experiences and her communication style.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The floors are sticky, the air smells like desperation and well liquor, and I'm fairly certain that rash is contagious.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: On the bright side, the free appetizers are below room temperature, which slows bacterial growth.

jokes.text: Crap. / We are going to the Glitter Factory. / What? / I can't go back there. But if you see Jasmine, tell her she can keep Anthony, but I want my microwave back.
jokes.setup: Leslie sees Tom needs extreme cheering up; the strip club (Glitter Factory) was the destination she'd earlier resisted
jokes.punchline: Someone's immediate objection that they 'can't go back there' — with a very specific backstory involving Jasmine, Anthony, and a microwave
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'tell her she can keep Anthony, but I want my microwave back' does a lot of work — it implies an entire complicated social drama with the strip club staff. The comedy is in what's left unsaid. Good character economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I want a woman who can open her own jars. That's all I'm asking for. I don't need her to talk to me. I don't need her to laugh at my jokes. But she better be able to open a jar.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm thinking Serena Williams. Venus Williams. Maybe a young Steffi Graf.

jokes.text: I can't go back there. But if you see Jasmine, tell her she can keep Anthony, but I want my microwave back.
jokes.setup: Leslie declares they're going to the Glitter Factory (strip club) to cheer up Tom.
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals he can't return to the strip club — not for moral reasons but because of a complex relationship situation involving Jasmine, Anthony, and a microwave.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. Ron has an entire relationship drama at the strip club — a woman named Jasmine, a man named Anthony he lost her to, and his primary concern is recovering a microwave. The hierarchy of his concerns (not the woman, the appliance) is perfect Ron Swanson. The specificity of all three names grounds the absurdity in apparent reality. This is one of the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That was the worst acting I've ever seen. You looked like a child trying to cry at a movie.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Anyway, I'm starving. What's for breakfast?

jokes.text: Good. You're gonna take April home. / No, I want to go to the Glitter Factory. / Drop out of school and start doing meth.
jokes.setup: Ron is trying to decide who's responsible enough to go to the strip club
jokes.punchline: When April protests, Ron responds by suggesting she drop out of school and do meth — an absurdly extreme 'if you insist on bad decisions' escalation
jokes.explanation: Pure Ron Swanson. His parental advice to April — 'Drop out of school and start doing meth' — is delivered as a logical escalation of her bad decision-making, treating it as an equivalence. The deadpan is everything here. Extremely high character integration and economy. Very quotable — this line is a classic Parks and Rec moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, you need to dial back the fake sadness. You're overacting.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? I'm not overacting.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You look like Leonardo DiCaprio in every movie he's ever been in.

jokes.text: I'm a feminist. I would never, ever go to a strip club. I've gone on record that if I had to have a stripper's name, it would be Equality. But I'm willing to sacrifice all that I've worked for just to put a smile on your perverted little face. So don't blow this.
jokes.setup: Leslie is about to enter a strip club despite her feminist principles
jokes.punchline: She frames her strip club visit as a profound moral sacrifice — and her chosen stripper name being 'Equality' is the central absurdist detail
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes and a genuine Parks and Rec all-timer. The setup (Leslie's feminist credentials), the absurdist detail (stripper name would be 'Equality'), the earnest self-sacrifice framing, and the practical button ('So don't blow this') are perfectly assembled. The stripper name 'Equality' is inspired — it's simultaneously on-brand and completely absurd. Very high character integration: this joke could only be Leslie Knope. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, I won? I thought I was playing pool!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Did I do that thing where you hit the white ball and then... no, that doesn't sound right.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Is 'sinking the eight ball' good or bad? Because I feel like I just got really lucky by accident.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm just gonna pretend I knew what I was doing the whole time.

jokes.text: Lap dances are on me. I mean, I'm paying for them. They're not gonna actually be on me.
jokes.setup: Leslie is being magnanimous about the strip club experience
jokes.punchline: She immediately clarifies her idiom — 'on me' — fearing a literal interpretation, which is actually funnier than the original confusion
jokes.explanation: The self-correction joke works well. Leslie's anxious over-clarification of a perfectly normal idiom in a strip club context reveals her discomfort while also delivering a good double-meaning joke. The structure is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so I own Ann now, right? Like, legally?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's not how this works, man.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But you said if I won the pool bet, Ann would be mine.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm not a prize, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, I know. But why doesn't it feel real then? I have the receipt.

jokes.text: I kind of feel like Jane Goodall studying the chimps. 'Cause there are some feminist scholars who say that stripping is a feminist act.
jokes.setup: Leslie is inside the strip club, trying to square her presence with her values
jokes.punchline: She reframes herself as an academic researcher (Jane Goodall) and reaches for a convenient feminist justification — the intellectual gymnastics are the joke
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy. Leslie's ability to find an academic justification for anything she wants to do is perfectly in character. The Jane Goodall comparison is both pompous and specific, which elevates it above a generic 'feminist scholar' reference.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, your name is Secretariat?

dialogue.speaker: Sierra
dialogue.line: No, it's Sierra.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I thought you said Secretariat, like the famous racehorse!

jokes.text: There is a girl here that also works at Quiznos. She's really nice to me here but really mean to me at Quiznos.
jokes.setup: The group is taking in the strip club environment
jokes.punchline: Jerry recognizes a dancer from Quiznos and has noticed a professional personality split between her two jobs — delivered with complete sincerity and no self-awareness
jokes.explanation: A superb Jerry joke. The observation itself is funny (the same person treats him differently in two professional contexts), but what makes it great is what it implies: Jerry is a Quiznos regular, he's been to the Glitter Factory enough to recognize a dancer, and he processes both interactions on the same professional customer-service level. Zero self-awareness. Rich in character and deeply funny. One of Jerry's best moments.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so I need you to take off your clothes, but I want you to know that I respect you as a woman and as a professional. You have agency, you have rights, and your body is a temple. Now, can you angle yourself slightly to the left? The light is better over there.

jokes.text: Go put these in places I do not approve of. / I'm gonna put these in places you've never heard of.
jokes.setup: Leslie has given Tom money for the strip club, with resigned disapproval
jokes.punchline: Tom escalates her disapproval into complete anatomical ignorance — 'places you've never heard of'
jokes.explanation: A clean two-line joke with great economy. Tom's response tops Leslie's disapproving framing with something genuinely funnier — implying the strip club involves anatomy Leslie isn't familiar with. The exchange works as a character duet.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, Seabiscuit, you can go.

jokes.text: Yeah, I've been a little down. Totally natural. I'm getting divorced. But now I'm ready to pull myself up by some g-strings.
jokes.setup: Tom addresses the camera at the strip club, performing his sad-about-divorce narrative
jokes.punchline: 'Pull myself up by some g-strings' — a pun on 'bootstraps' and underwear, delivered with Tom's trademark slick confidence
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed pun. 'Pull myself up by some g-strings' works as wordplay and as character comedy — Tom can't help being slick even when performing misery. The transition from performed sadness to strip club excitement in one sentence is a good joke arc.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I had a stripper as my emergency contact for like three years. I thought it was genius because she was always available, she was flexible with her schedule, and she knew how to handle money.

jokes.text: It's rough in here. Is it always like this? / I wouldn't know. Don't like strip clubs. Smells like a wet mop in here. And I get the feeling that these women is running a low-grade fever.
jokes.setup: Ann and Ron are taking in the strip club environment
jokes.punchline: Ron's assessment: the smell of a wet mop, and a medical concern that the dancers are running low-grade fevers — delivered with a physician's clinical concern and no prurient interest whatsoever
jokes.explanation: Ron Swanson in a strip club is already a great premise, but his reaction is perfectly calibrated: he notices a wet mop smell and is medically concerned about the performers' health. Not aroused, not morally judgmental — just clinically assessing the environmental and health conditions. 'These women is running a low-grade fever' is exceptional. This joke could only be Ron. One of the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know exactly how you feel. When Planet Earth ended, I was devastated for weeks. I couldn't eat, I couldn't sleep. I just kept thinking, 'What am I supposed to do now? I've seen all the penguins.'

jokes.text: Strippers do nothing for me. I like a strong, salt of the earth, self-possessed woman at the top of her field, your Steffi Grafs, your Sheryl Swoopes. But I will take a free breakfast buffet any time, any place.
jokes.setup: Ron is at a strip club, apparently unmoved
jokes.punchline: His ideal woman is an elite athlete in her prime (Steffi Graf, Sheryl Swoopes), but what actually excites him is a free breakfast buffet — discovered at the strip club
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes and a Ron Swanson all-timer. The construction is near-perfect: he delivers a sophisticated, surprisingly specific account of his ideal woman (elite female athletes), building expectations of complexity — then obliterates it with 'But I will take a free breakfast buffet any time, any place.' The pivot is perfectly timed, and the breakfast buffet at a strip club is an inspired detail. The specificity of Steffi Graf and Sheryl Swoopes elevates it far above a generic 'Ron loves food' joke. This approaches elite sitcom comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, how could you ask out Wendy? She's terrible! She's mean, she's dismissive, she makes fun of people for no reason.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I don't see what the problem is.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The problem is she's awful! And you're... you're wonderful. And now I have to watch you with her, and it's going to be torture. I'm going to have to see you two together, and I'm going to lose my mind. I'm going to start screaming at work. They're going to have to remove me from the building. I'll lose my job. I won't be able to pay my rent. I'll end up living in my car. And then my car will break down, and I'll be living on the street. And then I'll get sick from living on the street, and I'll die alone and cold and afraid, and I'll wish I was never born.

jokes.text: Does she make scrambled eggs?
jokes.setup: Leslie is asking Ron whether he wants to pursue Wendy seriously
jokes.punchline: Ron's primary romantic criterion for Wendy is whether she makes scrambled eggs — delivered in complete earnest
jokes.explanation: A perfect four-word callback to the breakfast buffet joke. Ron's romantic interest in Wendy is filtered entirely through his breakfast food enthusiasm, and it's one of the episode's best moments. The economy is exceptional — four words that reveal an entire worldview. Only works because the buffet joke immediately preceded it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, can you carry him?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: He weighs as much as a bale of hay.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Just lift with your legs, not your back.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm like a beautiful, tiny man.

jokes.text: Take it down a notch. You already won your Oscar, DiCaprio.
jokes.setup: Tom has been over-performing his sadness to the point where it's become theatrical
jokes.punchline: Ron's critique of Tom's acting uses a very specific cultural reference — 'you already won your Oscar, DiCaprio' — as a note to dial it back
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical line. Ron calling Tom 'DiCaprio' implies he's recognized the performance as acting, and the 'you already won your Oscar' framing suggests the performance was effective enough but now is being overdone. The joke works as both a directing note and a character beat for Ron — he's been in on the deception and is managing it professionally.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wendy, I have concerns about the men coming over to your house at all hours. It's inappropriate and frankly, it makes you look like a trollop!

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: A trollop? Did you just call me a trollop?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes! A trollop! A woman of loose morals! A strumpet! A harlot of the night!

jokes.text: Ann, in case I don't sink this, it's been a real pleasure dating you. (Andy's pre-game goodbye before the decisive pool shot)
jokes.setup: Andy is about to take a crucial pool shot that will determine whether he 'wins' Ann
jokes.punchline: He delivers a dramatic farewell to Ann as if about to die — treating a pool game like a final heroic act
jokes.explanation: A sweet and funny character moment. Andy treating the pool shot with wartime gravity is in character, and 'it's been a real pleasure dating you' acknowledges his genuine feelings for Ann through the absurd competition framing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, Wendy, I have an idea for a new club. It's called 'The Betrayers,' and it's a support group for people who've been betrayed by someone they trusted. You two should definitely be charter members.

jokes.text: Scratch on the eight! I'm victorious. I'm awesome at pool, and I hustled your ass.
jokes.setup: Andy's been losing catastrophically throughout; his hustle plan has completely failed
jokes.punchline: Mark accidentally scratches on the eight ball, giving Andy the win through pure luck — which Andy immediately attributes to his own skill and hustle
jokes.explanation: A great payoff to the hustle storyline. Andy wins through a fluke, then immediately takes full credit for a masterful hustle. 'I'm awesome at pool, and I hustled your ass' is delivered with complete sincerity after being $6,400 in debt. The callback pays off the whole arc.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I feel like I'm dying. My head is pounding, my mouth tastes like a tire fire, and I'm pretty sure my liver filed for divorce.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But I found the cure. It's called a Tommy Fresh Detox Smoothie. It's got activated charcoal, wheatgrass, and a little bit of that fancy mineral water from that place in Iceland.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: One sip and I'll be—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: *vomits immediately*

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? It worked.

jokes.text: Take a moment to say good-bye. I don't even know how to say this. I am so sorry, and I will do my best to visit you on holidays. / Thanks. You tried. / I guess you're his now.
jokes.setup: Andy has 'won' Ann in the pool bet; Mark must cede her
jokes.punchline: Mark accepts the outcome like it's a real transaction — encouraging Andy to say goodbye, apologizing, promising holiday visits — and then 'I guess you're his now' to Ann
jokes.explanation: The absurdist payoff of actually going through with the 'Ann as prize' joke. Mark genuinely acting like he's handing over custody of a person is very funny, and 'I guess you're his now' said to Ann is a great line. The scene works because everyone plays it completely straight.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you're not even actually Canadian?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, I'm from Canada. Technically I was born in Toronto.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? But you grew up in Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, my parents moved here when I was three months old. I've been a citizen since I was five.

jokes.text: I know that legally Ann is now mine, but it weirdly doesn't feel that way. (Andy's confessional)
jokes.setup: Andy has 'won' Ann in the pool bet but Ann has walked off with Mark
jokes.punchline: Andy acknowledges the 'legal' ownership (of a person) while noting the discrepancy between the contract and reality
jokes.explanation: A great button to the pool storyline. The phrase 'legally Ann is now mine' treats a pool bet as legally binding contract over a human being — Andy's complete sincerity about this is the joke. His bafflement at the gap between 'legal' ownership and reality is excellent character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Please don't say 'psych' anymore. It's really annoying.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, I won't say it anymore. Psych!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, I'm sorry. I appreciate that you remembered that that's my thing.

jokes.text: This is Seabiscuit. / Sierra. / Sorry, it's loud in here. And I gave her money to writhe around on your parts.
jokes.setup: Leslie has hired a dancer for Tom and is introducing her
jokes.punchline: She gets the name wrong (Seabiscuit instead of Sierra), apologizes for the noise, then describes the transaction as 'writhe around on your parts' — an extremely clinical/awkward description of a lap dance
jokes.explanation: A cluster of good Leslie jokes. Calling the dancer 'Seabiscuit' (a racehorse name) by mistake, then the awkward cover 'sorry, it's loud,' then 'writhe around on your parts' — each component adds to the picture of Leslie being hilariously out of her depth. 'Your parts' as a euphemism is particularly good.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Bye, Ann. You're the best. Bye, Pancakes.

jokes.text: This is Seabiscuit. / Sierra. / Sorry, it's loud in here. And I gave her money to writhe around on your parts.
jokes.setup: Leslie is introducing a performer to Tom for a lap dance.
jokes.punchline: Leslie mishears the performer's name as 'Seabiscuit' (a racehorse) and then describes the lap dance in the most clinical, bloodless terms possible — 'writhe around on your parts.'
jokes.explanation: Leslie calling a stripper 'Seabiscuit' is great — both as an accidental name and as a subconscious equine metaphor. But the real punchline is 'writhe around on your parts' — Leslie's clinical description of what a lap dance entails, reducing it to its technical elements, is pure Leslie-processing-something-unfamiliar.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, you like Wendy? Like, romantically?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wendy? Our Wendy?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The woman?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yes, Andy, the woman.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: With the... face?

jokes.text: Really grind the sorrow out of him. And then afterwards, reconsider your profession, but for now, grind away.
jokes.setup: Leslie is instructing a dancer how to give Tom a lap dance
jokes.punchline: She frames the lap dance as a therapeutic procedure, then undercuts it by telling the dancer to reconsider her career — but only after finishing the job
jokes.explanation: An excellent Leslie Knope joke. The line does so much simultaneously: she frames the lap dance in therapeutic terms ('grind the sorrow out'), maintains her feminist concern by asking the dancer to reconsider her profession, but then pragmatically insists on the service first ('but for now, grind away'). The structure is impeccable — earnest concern bracketing practical necessity. Highly quotable, very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I still have glitter on me. It's like I'm a disco ball.

jokes.text: Stripper dancing action. (stage direction read aloud / confessional describing the visual)
jokes.setup: The dancer is performing a lap dance for Tom
jokes.punchline: The transcript/scene is described simply as 'Stripper dancing action' — either a deadpan confessional from Tom narrating his own lap dance, or a stage direction that became a moment
jokes.explanation: A brief comedic beat — whether Tom is narrating or this is a visual description of what's happening, the blandness of 'stripper dancing action' as a descriptor is mildly funny. Not exceptional but registers.

jokes.text: I don't want to do this. / Is it because you have a strong, positive, female figure watching you? / No, it's because I'm miserable. / Never mind. Thank you, Seabiscuit. That'll be all.
jokes.setup: Tom is receiving a lap dance but is genuinely unhappy
jokes.punchline: Leslie assumes Tom's discomfort is because of her feminist presence — then, upon learning he's actually miserable, immediately dismisses the dancer with a second 'Seabiscuit' mistake
jokes.explanation: Great joke construction. Leslie's initial assumption ('Is it because you have a strong, positive, female figure watching you?') reveals her self-importance, the pivot to genuine emotion punctures the comedy, and then 'Never mind. Thank you, Seabiscuit.' returns both the Seabiscuit callback AND Leslie's breezy managerial efficiency. Multiple layers working simultaneously.

jokes.text: Never mind. Thank you, Seabiscuit. That'll be all.
jokes.setup: Tom has admitted genuine sadness and Leslie is calling off the lap dance.
jokes.punchline: Leslie dismisses the performer by the wrong name again — 'Seabiscuit' — with the formal register of dismissing a butler, 'That'll be all.'
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'Seabiscuit' pays off — Leslie still hasn't learned the name. 'That'll be all' as a Victorian dismissal in a strip club is a good tonal joke. Short, clean, works as a button.

jokes.text: I've been to the Glitter Factory a million times. That girl up there, she's my emergency contact. But right now, I hate it here. And I just want to see Wendy.
jokes.setup: Tom breaks down emotionally at the strip club
jokes.punchline: The revelation that a Glitter Factory dancer is Tom's emergency contact — delivered as a factual aside in an emotional moment
jokes.explanation: A great character revelation. The emotional sincerity of Tom's breakdown is punctured and deepened by 'that girl up there, she's my emergency contact' — which tells us everything about Tom's social world in seven words. It's funny and poignant simultaneously, which is Parks and Rec at its best.

jokes.text: It's perfectly normal to feel devastated when something's over. It's exactly how I felt when that Planet Earth series ended.
jokes.setup: Leslie is comforting Tom about the genuine grief of his marriage ending
jokes.punchline: She equates divorce grief with the sadness of a documentary series ending — completely in earnest
jokes.explanation: A top-tier Leslie Knope joke. The structure is perfect: she begins with genuine, warm wisdom ('it's perfectly normal to feel devastated when something's over') — then reveals her reference point for devastating loss is a nature documentary ending. The comedy is in the complete earnestness and the proportionality failure. Very high character integration, very quotable. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: 60 days! And then she's free to marry Ron Swanson. / What? Ron? / He's gonna ask her out. He told me.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to help Tom accept the divorce
jokes.punchline: Leslie casually reveals Ron has romantic plans for Wendy — blindsiding Tom and escalating the emotional stakes
jokes.explanation: A solid plot beat played for comedy. The casual '60 days! And then she's free to marry Ron Swanson' is a funny compression of Leslie's pragmatic approach to Tom's grief. Her matter-of-fact delivery of Ron's romantic plans to a vulnerable Tom is obliviously funny.

jokes.text: What is wrong with you? I wish I wasn't alive to hear myself say this, but I am ashamed to be your deputy.
jokes.setup: Leslie confronts Ron about planning to pursue Wendy while Tom is still emotionally raw
jokes.punchline: 'I wish I wasn't alive to hear myself say this' — Leslie prefaces her disappointment in Ron with a dramatic disclaimer about her own suffering in having to express it
jokes.explanation: Strong Leslie line. 'I wish I wasn't alive to hear myself say this' is a beautifully hyperbolic self-aware disclaimer — she's devastated by her own emotion here. The inversion (she's ashamed of HIM but suffering through saying it) is well-constructed.

jokes.text: I don't get men. If they're not wagering their girlfriends in pool, then they're trying to steal each other's wives. It makes you question the whole notion of those bromance movies.
jokes.setup: Leslie is processing both the pool bet incident and Ron's Wendy situation simultaneously
jokes.punchline: She connects the two male behaviors under one rubric and concludes it undermines the bromance genre — a completely logical but absurd conclusion
jokes.explanation: A good recap joke that earns laughs from connecting two separate plots. 'It makes you question the whole notion of those bromance movies' is a funny non-sequitur conclusion that's also very Leslie.

jokes.text: I don't get men. If they're not wagering their girlfriends in pool, then they're trying to steal each other's wives. It makes you question the whole notion of those bromance movies.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just discovered both the pool bet (Andy wagering Ann) and Ron's plan to pursue Wendy.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's generalization — connecting both plots to a critique of 'bromance movies' — is a perfectly Leslie intellectualization of chaos, and the pivot to 'bromance movies' is an absurd but logical Leslie conclusion.
jokes.explanation: A good meta-observation that ties both subplots together thematically. 'Bromance movies' is an unexpected conclusion that reveals Leslie's cultural reference points and her tendency to academicize everything.

jokes.text: Could you carry him out of here? And, you know, also maybe not have sex with his wife? Thanks. / From the knees. He weighs eight pounds.
jokes.setup: Tom has passed out drunk; Leslie needs Ron to carry him and is also still annoyed about Wendy
jokes.punchline: Leslie's breathless 'also maybe not have sex with his wife? Thanks' as a casual addendum, followed by Ron's purely logistical 'from the knees, he weighs eight pounds'
jokes.explanation: A great double-punch exchange. Leslie's 'also maybe not have sex with his wife?' is a brilliantly casual way of delivering a serious request — the 'Thanks' makes it perfect. Ron's pivot to the mechanics of carrying Tom ('from the knees, he weighs eight pounds') is pure Ron: he acknowledges the real concern with action, not words. 'He weighs eight pounds' is also a great joke about Tom's build.

jokes.text: My God. You insensitive little hussy. Excuse me? / Halt.
jokes.setup: Leslie, Ann, and Ron arrive at Wendy's apartment carrying the passed-out Tom. Wendy opens the door with another man present.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately calls Wendy an 'insensitive little hussy' for having a male visitor, then shouts 'Halt' to the man
jokes.explanation: 'Insensitive little hussy' is a wonderful anachronistic insult from Leslie — perfectly in character (she'd use the word 'hussy') — and 'Halt' as a command to a stranger is hilariously formal. Good cringe setup for what follows.

jokes.text: You're not divorced yet and you're inviting other men over? / You're married? / Technically, yeah. / That's my husband. / Who's he carrying? / No. That's his boss. My husband's the one that's being carried. By his boss.
jokes.setup: The group arrives at Wendy's door with an unconscious Tom; a stranger is in the apartment
jokes.punchline: The escalating confusion — 'that's my husband' / 'who's he carrying?' / 'no, that's his boss, my husband's the one being carried, by his boss' — builds perfectly as each clarification makes things stranger
jokes.explanation: The explanatory dialogue is structured like a perfect comedy escalation: each clarification is stranger than the last, culminating in 'my husband's the one that's being carried. By his boss.' The rhythm is excellent, and the visual implied (Ron carrying tiny Tom) makes the delivery even funnier.

jokes.text: You know what? You and Ron will be perfect for each other. You should get married and start a club for people who betray Tom Haverford.
jokes.setup: Leslie is furious at both Wendy (for having a guest) and Ron (for planning to pursue Wendy)
jokes.punchline: She suggests they form a 'club for people who betray Tom Haverford' — framing betrayal as a shared hobby that would bond them
jokes.explanation: A sharp Leslie line. The 'club for people who betray Tom Haverford' as an organizing principle is a funny concept — treating a personal affront like a civic organization. Very in character for someone who organizes everything.

jokes.text: You have a lovely home. (Ron, to Wendy, while carrying the unconscious Tom)
jokes.setup: An extremely chaotic and emotionally charged scene at Wendy's door
jokes.punchline: Ron, in the middle of all this, pauses to offer a sincere, polite compliment on the home
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Five words, maximum impact. Ron — while carrying an unconscious man to his estranged wife's apartment in the middle of chaos — smoothly transitions to a sincere home compliment. It's simultaneously a character reveal (he's interested in Wendy and is already being charming) and a sublime deadpan understatement. The timing and economy are exceptional. Very high character integration: only Ron Swanson would do this in this moment.

jokes.text: You know those hangover pills you can order on TV? I threw up a bunch of them this morning and feel much better.
jokes.setup: The morning after, Leslie checks on Tom's hangover
jokes.punchline: Tom's hangover cure is throwing up the hangover pills — which presumably means they didn't work — but he reports feeling 'much better'
jokes.explanation: A solid joke about the absurdity of as-seen-on-TV remedies and Tom's consumer gullibility. The twist — he threw them up — as a positive outcome is a good contradiction. Very Tom to order TV products.

jokes.text: My God, because you're Libyan. / No, damn it. Wendy's from Canada.
jokes.setup: Tom reveals his marriage to Wendy was a green-card arrangement
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately assumes Tom is the immigrant in need of a green card, guessing Libya; Tom's exasperated correction — 'Wendy's from Canada' — reveals Leslie's assumption was both wrong and oddly specific
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection and character comedy. Leslie's 'because you're Libyan' — implying she had a fully developed theory about Tom's immigration status — is funnier than any more logical guess. Tom's 'No, damn it. Wendy's from Canada' is the perfect exasperated correction. Two punchlines in one exchange: the wrong country, and the anticlimactic real answer (Canada). Great structure.

jokes.text: I hope I'm not gonna have to explain to you that you don't own me. / Of course not. I never for one second thought that that was for real.
jokes.setup: Andy has 'won' Ann in the pool bet and now speaks to her the morning after
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately disclaims any belief that the bet was real — but we know from his confessional that he absolutely believed it was
jokes.explanation: A good callback to Andy's confessional where he absolutely believed he legally owned Ann. His hasty denial when confronted is a solid character beat, and Ann's suspicion is warranted given his behavior.

jokes.text: If you say 'psych', I'm gonna be really pissed. / You remembered how much I like to say 'psych'.
jokes.setup: Andy is sincerely letting Ann go; she's suspicious of a bait-and-switch
jokes.punchline: Andy's response to her suspicion isn't denial but warmth — 'you remembered how much I like to say psych' — treating her knowledge of his habits as a sign of connection
jokes.explanation: A lovely character moment for Andy. The joke is that he hears 'you remembered how much I like to say psych' as an affectionate callback rather than an accusation — it briefly gives him hope. It's sweet and funny simultaneously, which is Andy Dwyer's specialty.

jokes.text: If you say 'psych', I'm gonna be really pissed. / You remembered how much I like to say 'psych'.
jokes.setup: Andy is saying something genuinely heartfelt to Ann about leaving her and Mark alone.
jokes.punchline: Ann interrupts to worry about 'psych' because Andy has historically used the word — and Andy's delighted response to being remembered for this trait reveals it as a point of pride.
jokes.explanation: A sweet, character-rich beat — Ann knowing Andy well enough to fear a 'psych,' and Andy being touched that she remembers this about him. The inversion of his usual cluelessness (he's aware she knows him) is a nice twist.

jokes.text: I thought for a second you were gonna chase after me, but you didn't. / I meant every word I said.
jokes.setup: Andy has said a genuine goodbye to Ann and she's walked away.
jokes.punchline: Ann's admission that she expected Andy to chase her — and his response that he meant it — is a character reversal joke: Andy, usually chaotic, is sincere, and Ann is the one who had low expectations.
jokes.explanation: A warm character beat more than a joke, but it functions as a comedic payoff — the expectation (Andy will do something dumb) is subverted (he doesn't). The laugh is mild but the character work is good.

jokes.text: You like your wife? That's a bummer. / Anyone knows that you like your wife? Your wife knows that you like your wife? / I didn't know until yesterday. So don't tell anyone. Don't tell Ron.
jokes.setup: Mark reveals to Tom that he actually has feelings for Ann
jokes.punchline: Tom's reaction to Mark's emotional revelation is 'You like your wife? That's a bummer' — treating real romantic feelings for one's own partner as a problem to be managed. Then: 'Your wife knows that you like your wife?'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best constructed moments. 'You like your wife? That's a bummer' is a perfect distillation of Tom's worldview — genuine romantic feelings are a liability, not an asset. The follow-up questions escalate the absurdity perfectly: 'Anyone knows that you like your wife? Your wife knows that you like your wife?' Each question frames spousal affection as a shameful secret to be managed. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: How could there possibly still be glitter on me? Takes forever to get off. My crotch looks like a disco ball.
jokes.setup: The morning after the Glitter Factory visit
jokes.punchline: Leslie has strip club glitter on her person, specifically describing her crotch as 'a disco ball' — an image that is both vivid and mortifying for a feminist public servant
jokes.explanation: A great closing character joke. The image of earnest feminist Leslie Knope describing her crotch as a disco ball due to strip club glitter is funny, quotable, and a satisfying callback to the Glitter Factory storyline. 'Takes forever to get off' as a technical problem Leslie is processing is very in character.

jokes.text: Sorry she called you selfish of course / She just didn't know the full story of course / But now that she does she's sorry of course / She loves being your deputy — The Mr. Ed parody reprise
jokes.setup: The episode ends with a resolution between Leslie and Ron
jokes.punchline: Leslie brings back her Mr. Ed divorce parody song, now rewritten to apologize to Ron — using the same ridiculous vehicle for an earnest reconciliation
jokes.explanation: A warm callback that works both comedically and emotionally. The joke is that Leslie's method of sincere apology is the same Mr. Ed parody format — she's consistent in her absurdity. It's an affectionate closing to the episode that reinforces Leslie and Ron's dynamic.

tmdb_overview: After Leslie finds out that Tom is getting a divorce, the department takes him out on the town to cheer him up. Meanwhile, Andy tries to hustle Mark in a game of pool.
insight: Tom's divorce spawns 66 jokes in 24 minutes—the show's densest half-hour to date.
